title: Endoscopic Retrograde Cholangiopancreatography (ERCP)
subject: Medicine
summary: ERCP combines endoscopy and fluoroscopy to visualise and treat biliary and pancreatic duct disease. In low‑resource settings it remains the main therapeutic tool for obstructive jaundice, cholangitis and selected pancreatic leaks.

sections.p: ERCP is a minimally invasive procedure that uses a side‑viewing duodenoscope to inject contrast into the biliary and pancreatic ducts under fluoroscopic guidance.
b: Provides both imaging and therapeutic options in one session
Requires sedation, fluoroscopy, and skilled endoscopist

sections.p: Severity is judged by the underlying disease (e.g., cholangitis grade, stone burden) and by procedure‑related risk (e.g., pancreatitis, perforation).
b: Tokyo Guidelines grade A–C cholangitis guides urgency of ERCP
Large stones (>10 mm) or multiple stones increase technical difficulty

sections.p: Obstruction of the common bile duct is the commonest indication for ERCP in East Africa.
b: Choledocholithiasis – most frequent cause of obstructive jaundice
Strictures from primary sclerosing cholangitis, cholangiocarcinoma, or post‑operative scarring
Parasite‑related obstruction (e.g., Fasciola hepatica) – region‑specific
HIV‑related opportunistic biliary disease (e.g., CMV cholangitis)

sections.p: Patients present with jaundice, right upper quadrant pain, fever, or pancreatitis depending on the level and duration of obstruction.
b: Charcot’s triad (fever, RUQ pain, jaundice) suggests acute cholangitis
Elevated alkaline phosphatase and bilirubin point to biliary obstruction
Persistent epigastric pain with lipase rise may indicate post‑ERCP pancreatitis

t.b: Detects dilated intra‑hepatic ducts and stones; if unavailable, rely on clinical jaundice and liver function tests

t.a: Liver function tests (ALT, AST, ALP, GGT, bilirubin)
t.b: Confirms cholestasis; a rising bilirubin >5 mg/dL signals urgent ERCP
Excludes mass lesions and assesses for pancreatic necrosis
Answers the question ‘What is the exact level and cause of ductal obstruction?’; contrast filling defects = stones, strictures appear as narrowed segments
Identify causative organism in cholangitis; guide antibiotics before ERCP

sections.p: Complications can be life‑threatening and must be recognised early.
b: Post‑ERCP pancreatitis – most common; watch for abdominal pain and rising amylase after 24 h
Severe cholangitis – fever, hypotension, mental status change; requires urgent drainage
Perforation – sudden severe pain, free air on X‑ray
Bleeding from sphincterotomy – hematemesis or melena

sections.p: Therapeutic ERCP aims to relieve obstruction and treat infection while minimising complications.
b: Antibiotics (e.g., ceftriaxone) before and after ERCP for cholangitis; avoid aminoglycosides in renal impairment
Sphincterotomy followed by stone extraction with basket or balloon for stones ≤10 mm
Large stones: mechanical lithotripsy or temporary stent placement if lithotripsy unavailable
Stricture dilation and placement of plastic or metal stent; metal stents preferred for malignant strictures
If ERCP fails or fluoroscopy unavailable, percutaneous transhepatic drainage is an alternative

sections.p: After successful ERCP, monitor for delayed pancreatitis and ensure ductal patency.
b: Check liver enzymes 24–48 h; persistent elevation may need repeat imaging
Educate patients on avoiding biliary sludge (dietary fat moderation, treat gallstones early)
Vaccinate against hepatitis B to reduce future cholangiopathy in endemic areas

sections.p: Conditions that mimic biliary obstruction clinically.
b: Acute hepatitis – presents with jaundice but lacks ductal dilatation
Pancreatic head cancer – may cause painless jaundice; requires CT/MRI for differentiation
Mirizzi syndrome – gallstone impacted in cystic duct compressing common bile duct

sections.p: Interpretation pitfalls specific to low‑resource settings.
b: Normal bilirubin does not exclude early cholangitis; rely on fever and RUQ pain
Ultrasound may miss small stones; a negative scan should not delay ERCP if clinical suspicion is high
Fluoroscopy quality may be poor; subtle strictures can be overlooked – consider repeat study if symptoms persist

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden severe abdominal pain after ERCP
High‑grade fever, hypotension, or altered mental status (severe cholangitis)
Persistent vomiting with rising amylase (post‑ERCP pancreatitis)

faq.q: Why is ERCP preferred over MRCP in emergencies?
faq.a: ERCP provides immediate therapeutic options (stone removal, stenting) while MRCP is diagnostic only.

faq.q: Can ERCP be done without fluoroscopy?
faq.a: In some centres a ‘pure endoscopic’ approach is used, but ductal visualization is limited and success rates fall.
Rectal NSAIDs (e.g., indomethacin) given immediately before the procedure lower the risk.

exam: A 45‑year‑old man with Charcot’s triad presents to a district hospital lacking MRCP – what is the next step and why? — Immediate ERCP for drainage because cholangitis is grade B‑C and delay increases mortality.

During ERCP a 12‑mm stone is seen; the endoscopist cannot extract it with a basket – what alternatives are appropriate in a low‑resource setting? — Place a temporary plastic stent to decompress the duct and arrange referral for lithotripsy or repeat ERCP.

A patient develops severe epigastric pain 6 h after ERCP; amylase is 3‑fold rise – how do you manage? — Admit, keep NPO, give IV fluids, analgesia, and monitor; most cases resolve with supportive care.
Why is a metal stent favoured over a plastic stent for malignant biliary obstruction? — Metal stents have longer patency (>6 months) and lower occlusion rates, reducing repeat procedures.

What are the key differences between ERCP‑related cholangitis and sepsis from a urinary source? — ERCP cholangitis shows biliary dilatation, elevated ALP, and often requires biliary drainage; urinary sepsis shows pyuria and needs catheter drainage.

Explain how you would differentiate Mirizzi syndrome from common bile duct stones on ultrasound. — Mirizzi shows a stone in the cystic duct causing extrinsic compression of the CBD, often with a normal CBD diameter proximal to the compression.

A patient with HIV on antiretroviral therapy presents with cholestatic LFTs; what opportunistic causes should you consider before ERCP? — CMV cholangitis, Mycobacterium avium complex, and fungal infections; treat medically if identified before invasive procedures.

What measures can you take if fluoroscopy is unavailable but ERCP is urgently needed? — Use a pure endoscopic approach with careful cannulation, limit contrast use, and arrange percutaneous drainage if drainage fails.
